strategy.headline: Six banners sell themselves. Nike's job is the cold walk to 1901 W. Madison.
strategy.thesis: Chicago treats the Bulls as a six-banner religion, so 1990s red-and-black sells through a 31-51 season and a ground-up rebuild without Nike lifting a finger. The upside is in what the market doesn't have yet. This city sorts itself by side, high school and grid number, and plays its winter ball in Park District fieldhouses. It also gave the world house, the Wall of Respect, JB skating and Chicago Imagism. It's early October and new apparel needs 9-12 months, so 2026-27 is a seeding year: existing Bulls product, partner introductions and wear-tests. This brief is the build plan for 2027-28. Let Jordan Brand own the dynasty, and make cold-weather outerwear the hero. Use Madison Street, where North and South addresses begin and the Bulls play, as the one-city story the Splitter-era core can grow into.

archetype.name: The Six-Banner Congregation
archetype.description: A multigenerational faith in the 1991-98 Bulls that spans every side of town. It keeps buying through losing seasons but meets every rebuild promise with South Side and West Side sarcasm. The banners and the red-and-black have its loyalty. The roster has to earn it.

pulse.teamMoment: Year one of a new regime. Billy Donovan stepped down, Tiago Splitter took over as coach, and EVP Bryson Graham is building a size-first 'SLAP' roster. The core is Josh Giddey, Matas Buzelis and No. 4 pick Caleb Wilson, with Norman Powell and Nic Claxton added. The Bulls are coming off 31-51, sit low in power rankings and have no opening-night or Christmas Day game. Their early national stage is Emirates NBA Cup East Group C, against Boston, Atlanta, Charlotte and Washington.
pulse.sentiment: Guarded hope under ownership fatigue. Fans like the draft and Wilson's First Team All-Summer League debut, but they've learned to mock hype and wait for proof.

topInsights.title: Heritage is the floor, not the growth
topInsights.insight: Jordan 23, Pippen 33 and Rodman 91 still rival current jerseys at the United Center. Every retail lens says heritage outsells the roster, whatever the record. The art lens warns that another '90s throwback cycle in a rebuild year reads as filler: the dynasty is the baseline, not the news.
topInsights.implication: Keep heritage as an evergreen layer, coordinated with Jordan Brand. Put new design energy into civic, neighborhood and new-core stories. Don't overbuy current-player inventory before Wilson proves himself.

topInsights.title: The Hawk writes the merchandise plan
topInsights.insight: The home season runs through the months when lake wind makes 20 degrees feel like zero. Fans ride the No. 20 Madison bus or walk a long, exposed stretch from the L, hoodie under the jersey and coat over it. Outdoor runs move into fieldhouses from November to April. Spending peaks between the first freeze and Dec 20.
topInsights.implication: Make three hero Bulls products: a coat built to go over a jersey, heavyweight fleece and a cuffed knit. Land them before the first freeze. Tees and shorts are a short June-to-August business.

topInsights.title: Madison Street: the team every side shares
topInsights.insight: Addresses count from State and Madison. The United Center sits at 1901 W. Madison, on the line between North and South addresses, while the Cubs and Sox split the city by side. Chicagoans place each other by side, grid number and 'Where'd you go to high school?'
topInsights.implication: Build grid-coordinate and street-sign product that adds up to one city. Lead with '1901 W' and the zero point, which only the Bulls can own. Leave area codes to the indie shops and street vendors who already own them.

topInsights.title: Black-built culture no other city can claim
topInsights.insight: House was named at The Warehouse on Jefferson, less than two miles east of the United Center. The South Side gave the country the Wall of Respect, AfriCOBRA's 'Kool-Aid colors', JB skating at The Rink on 87th, footwork and Simeon's Public League dynasty. No other NBA market can claim any of it.
topInsights.implication: These are the strongest stories Nike can design from, and they only work co-authored, named and paid. Keep two scenes out of Bulls product on purpose: skate (Wicker Park and Nike SB) and queer nightlife from Northalsted to South Shore. Both prize independence from team merch, so support them through their own organizers, not a Bulls logo.

topInsights.title: Jordan owns the shoe, rivals own the hometown heroes
topInsights.insight: Sneakerheads worldwide call the white, red and black AJ1 'Chicagos'. But several of the city's favorite sons and daughters sit with rival brands: Derrick Rose and Candace Parker with adidas, Joe Freshgoods with New Balance. Nike's local ties are Mac Irvin Fire (a Nike EYBL program), the Bulls and Sky uniforms, Jordan Brand's Don C lineage and boutique partners such as Notre.
topInsights.implication: Don't ship another white-red-black colorway, and don't borrow Rose's No. 1 or his Englewood story. Win with new materials and stories, grassroots investment in Park District gyms and boutique partners with Nike history.

topInsights.title: Lights-out is the Bulls' signature
topInsights.insight: The darkened arena, roving spotlights and starting-lineup intro came over from Chicago Stadium and survived into the rebuild. It's the team's best-known gameday moment, and fans use 'Sirius' as shorthand for the whole ritual.
topInsights.implication: Put reflective or glow Bulls-red beams on blackout bases, and pregame and warm-up product will feel made in the building. Don't license the song: never name it or use it on product.

topInsights.title: The rebuild has a hometown face and a second homeland
topInsights.insight: Buzelis is the young core's one Chicago-area native, and he's Lithuanian-American. The metro has one of the largest Lithuanian communities outside Lithuania, a country that treats basketball as a national religion. Chicago also has civic language for a size-first roster in Big Shoulders and 'I Will', so the rebuild can sell without hype words.
topInsights.implication: Build a Buzelis lane with Lithuanian-Chicago institutions and his family's blessing. For the core, use workwear 'build' textures and public-domain civic type instead of slogans. Stage rookie product after the first month, and keep the word 'rebuild' off product.

opportunities.title: Lake Wind: the coat over the jersey
opportunities.summary: A Bulls outerwear system for the January trip to 1901 W. Madison. It pairs a knee-length stadium coat cut to go over a jersey with heavyweight fleece, a cuffed knit and grip gloves in black, Bulls red and lake gray. In 2026-27, sell existing licensed outerwear and wear-test prototypes. The new system launches November 2027.
where: Bulls Team Store at the United Center
Nike app and online for out-of-city fans
opportunities.when: Winter 2026-27: push existing outerwear from early November to Dec 20. Wear-test prototypes with season-ticket holders through February. Drop the new system as the hero in the first week of November 2027.
opportunities.how: Prove it works before launch. Spend a winter wear-testing with season-ticket holders on the No. 20 Madison bus and the walk from the L, and let their notes shape the 2027 coat. Keep 'Hawk' in the copy only. Tier from knit and gloves to fleece to coat, so the 10.25% city tax doesn't price out entry buyers.
opportunities.segment: Season-ticket families and suburban fans, plus dynasty diehards who wear a coat over the jersey
opportunities.kpi: Sell-through by price tier (entry, core, premium) by Dec 20 against last season, and wear-test ratings on warmth and fit over a jersey.

opportunities.title: Madison Street: one city, every side
opportunities.summary: A 2027-28 collection coded to the grid and built on the Bulls' own address. Think split North/South hoodies, '1901 W' shooting shirts and grid-coordinate caps in street-sign lettering. A single 708 south-suburb edition is the only area-code piece.
opportunities.when: Commission the type designer and muralist in winter 2026-27. Paint the mural in spring 2027, after the thaw. Launch the collection at the 2027-28 home opener and carry it through the holiday window.
opportunities.how: Commission a Chicago type designer for the street-sign lettering. Hire a South or West Side muralist, credited and paid, for a Wabash Arts Corridor wall that celebrates the city's sides, not individual players. Make the 708 edition with a south-suburb maker. Skip 630 and 847 unless a suburban partner asks for them.
opportunities.segment: Locals across all sides and the suburbs; tourists buying a Chicago-specific souvenir
opportunities.kpi: Sell-through by piece and door, and the share of sales from neighborhood and south-suburb doors outside the downtown corridor.

opportunities.title: Lights Out and the Basement Stock reissue
opportunities.summary: Pregame and boutique product for the new era. A near-black Spotlight warm-up carries reflective Bulls-red beams, and a roster tracklist tee runs in jersey numbers. A Nike-built 1990s half-zip in aged 'basement stock' red goes to taste-setting doors first.
opportunities.when: 2026-27: seed existing Bulls styles at boutique doors around the home opener and over Black Friday. 2027-28: launch the Spotlight warm-up and Basement Stock pieces at the home opener, and restock in December.
opportunities.how: Pair the launch with a mix by a paid local DJ and copy by Young Chicago Authors poets. Never use the intro song's name or audio. Keep the tracklist to numbers with no 'Rebuild' wording, and get NBPA clearance before any player names. Use original dot-matrix numerals. Run clean raffles, boutique first and big box second.
opportunities.segment: Gen Z digital fans, sneakerheads, vintage hunters and West Loop creatives
opportunities.kpi: Sell-out speed, raffle entries and resale premium as demand signals. Boutique reorder requests, and opener-week units against the 2026-27 seeding baseline.

opportunities.title: Buzelis and Lithuanian Chicago
opportunities.summary: A hometown lane for the core's Chicago-area native. In 2026-27, a community night with Lithuanian-Chicago institutions and bakeries. Then, in fall 2027, a small paid collaboration if he and the community want it.
opportunities.when: Community night around Lithuanian State Restoration Day (Feb 16, 2027). Collaboration at the start of 2027-28.
opportunities.how: First confirm Buzelis's community ties and get his family's blessing. Then build with the Balzekas Museum and community schools, and pay the bakeries that cater. Keep Lithuanian national symbols off Nike product unless the community and Lithuanian federation clear them. Route player use through the NBPA.
products: Community-night tee co-designed with a Lithuanian-Chicago artist
opportunities.segment: Lithuanian-American families across the city and southwest suburbs, and fans looking for a homegrown core player
opportunities.kpi: Community-night attendance and partner satisfaction, Buzelis jersey and tee sell-through in southwest-side and suburban doors, and partner interest in a second year.

opportunities.title: Fieldhouse City: Park District and Public League
opportunities.summary: Winter warm-ups in fieldhouse brick and varnished maple. First come donated floor refurbishments in South and West Side Park District gyms. School shooting shirts follow only where a school signs on.
where: Park District fieldhouses on the South and West Sides
Public League schools that opt in (Simeon, Whitney Young, Farragut, Marshall, Morgan Park)
opportunities.when: Donate and refurbish floors in winter 2026-27, with no product on them. Launch the Fieldhouse warm-up in January 2028. Time school shirts to the Public League city final, and a Downstate tee to March.
opportunities.how: Go in order. First, a donation-led floor refurbishment through the Park District's own approvals. Then licensed school shirts, only where a school and its athletic department sign, with proceeds to the program. Any documentary (Kartemquin or Coodie & Chike) follows a program with school, parent and IHSA clearance. Mac Irvin Fire stays the wear-test and Combine Week partner, outside the Public League story.
opportunities.segment: Teens, Public League families and neighborhood hoopers who claim players by school and side
opportunities.kpi: Floors refurbished and the league hours they host, dollars returned to school programs, and sell-through at neighborhood doors.

opportunities.title: Rink Session: the JB track suit
opportunities.summary: A stretch track suit co-designed with Chicago's JB skating crews, whose matching crew suits are already the city's own team uniform. The silhouette is ready and the partner is real. No other market has anything like it.
opportunities.when: Co-design with crews through 2026-27. Launch in late summer 2027 with a Bulls skate night at The Rink, ahead of the 2027-28 season.
opportunities.how: Pay crews as co-designers, embroider crew names where they want them, and let them set the skate-night program. Credit JB by name as a Black Chicago form. Make it a Bulls-licensed piece only if the crews and the Bulls agree.
opportunities.segment: JB crews, Black South Side families and style-setting dance and skate communities
opportunities.kpi: Track-suit sell-through in South Side doors, crew participation and content reach, and crew willingness to renew.

opportunities.title: Wall of Respect lineage: an AfriCOBRA commission
opportunities.summary: A named, licensed collaboration with surviving AfriCOBRA members and estates, whose movement included wearable art. Build it with the South Side Community Art Center and back it with year-round funding, not a February-only drop.
opportunities.when: Announce a year-round SSCAC fund in 2026-27. The artists set the product launch date: Black History Month is one option, not the default.
opportunities.how: License or commission named members and estates, with billing on the product and a revenue share, under SSCAC guidance. Never reproduce the 1967 Wall of Respect portraits, which carry likeness rights. Don't imitate the AfriCOBRA style without its artists.
opportunities.segment: Black Chicago from Bronzeville to the 708 south suburbs, and dynasty-era diehards
opportunities.kpi: Funding and proceeds delivered to SSCAC and artists. Sell-through in South Side and south-suburb doors against downtown, and artist willingness to renew.

opportunities.title: Born Here: house through the dead zone
opportunities.summary: A Nike-credited house collaboration with the Chosen Few DJs, in flag blue and Warehouse-flyer type. It carries no NBA marks, because house heritage isn't a Bulls property. It fills the Bulls' July-August dead zone with the city's own culture.
opportunities.when: Open the conversation in 2026-27. The Chosen Few set the release around their July 2027 picnic.
opportunities.how: Name the Chosen Few on the product, share revenue, credit house's Black and queer founders and consult the Knuckles estate. A separate Bulls house night at a home game needs Bulls approval. Frankie Knuckles Day stays with the house community unless Nike is invited.
products: 'Born in Chicago' house shooting shirt (Nike, no team marks)
opportunities.segment: House heads, Black South Side families and dance crews
opportunities.kpi: Summer revenue against an August baseline near zero, DJ and crew content reach, and Chosen Few interest in a second year.

collection.name: Big Shoulders
collection.story: Chicago calls itself the City of the Big Shoulders and 'The City That Works', and the new Bulls are being built on size and physicality. This 2027-28 collection holds the 1966 bull and the red-and-black fixed. It builds out from the city's working materials: the wind, the grid, the fieldhouse and the blackout before tip-off.

uniform.concept: Zero Point: 1901 W. Madison (pitch for the 2027-28 City Edition)
uniform.narrative: Every Chicago address counts out from State and Madison. The Bulls play on Madison, the line where North and South begin, which makes them the team every side shares in a city that splits its baseball. The uniform takes its code from the grid, the street sign and Sullivan's cast iron at the zero point. That gives the Splitter-era core a civic identity without leaning on the Jordan years. The 2026-27 set is locked, so pitch this to the Bulls and the NBA as the 2027-28 brief, after checking every past Bulls City Edition.
motifs: A hairline street-grid texture across the body, with the Madison line as a single red rule at the waist
Redrawn Sullivan ornament as a tonal black-on-black jacquard on the side panels
Hundred-block grid numbers ('1901 W') in the corner of the chest, like a Chicago street sign
Imagist-style line drawing on the matching warm-up and shooting shirt, commissioned from a Chicago artist
uniform.typography: A 'CHICAGO' wordmark in custom condensed street-sign capitals, drawn by a Chicago type designer. Bulls block numerals outlined in red and limestone, with small grid coordinates under the number.
details: Neck tape: '1901 W MADISON' in limestone
Jock tag: '0 N/S · 0 E/W', the State and Madison zero point
Waistband: NORTH · WEST · SOUTH in grid type, so the sides read as one line
Inner collar: 'I WILL', the public-domain 1890s civic motto
Court tie-in, as an idea only: grid lines along the sideline and the Madison line through center court. That's a Bulls and United Center call, in a building shared with the Blackhawks.
avoid: Full Chicago-flag prints, a fifth star, and any cue a past Bulls City Edition already used. Pull the full list before concepting.
The Jumpman, Jordan's name or likeness, or any implied Jordan co-sign without Jordan Brand
Six-point stars combined with crowns, pitchforks or other gang-nation symbols. Also 'Chiraq', drill references and violence imagery.
CTA signage, the City seal or Y-device, and CPS marks without clearance. Also brown honorary-street-sign tabs, which read as memorials to named people.
Any Native imagery: Chicago is Council of Three Fires homeland and the Blackhawks share the building

risks.risk: Colliding with Jordan Brand, which owns the dynasty, the 'Chicago' AJ1 and Jordan's name and likeness, or cannibalizing its sales.
risks.mitigation: Route all dynasty and Jumpman references through Jordan Brand. Give Nike Basketball's Bulls product new materials and civic stories, not another white-red-black one.

risks.risk: Rebuild hype backfires with skeptical fans who are tired of ownership and stuck with a low-rated roster.
risks.mitigation: Keep 'rebuild' and title-window talk off product, and use understated civic language. Keep current-player inventory lean until results justify more.

risks.risk: Exploiting or endangering communities. That covers drill, 'Chiraq' and gang-nation symbols, borrowed trade dress from Black-owned restaurants, AfriCOBRA style without its artists, and Latino neighborhoods under federal immigration enforcement.
risks.mitigation: Have community partners review every graphic and work only through named, paid, credited local authors. In Pilsen, Little Village and Humboldt Park, fund institutions rather than stage launches, and name no artist until they agree.

risks.risk: Hometown heroes on rival brands: Derrick Rose and Candace Parker with adidas, Joe Freshgoods with New Balance.
risks.mitigation: Never use their names, numbers or stories. Compete through Nike's own relationships (Mac Irvin Fire, the Bulls and Sky uniforms, boutique partners) and grassroots investment.

risks.risk: Third-party IP and slow approvals. Rights include the city flag, seal and Y device, CTA marks, CPS and IHSA marks, 'March Madness', the intro music and NBPA player rights. Approvals include the Park District board and Bulls-NBA sign-off on the City Edition and any court work.
risks.mitigation: Map every license and approval before concepting. Start the 2027-28 City Edition pitch and the Park District process now. Redraw rather than copy, and keep songs and trademarked phrases off product unless licensed.

scorecard.rationale: The six-banner heritage engine and a full flagship-to-mall network put Chicago second in the league on retail and top five on culture. A 31-51 rebuild and a 2027-28 build window hold opportunity and fandom nearer the middle (brief scores: opportunity 82, culture 93, retail 84, fandom 74). Chicago has one of the league's deepest design cultures, and it's a global heritage retail engine with a full network of flagship, arena, boutiques and suburban malls. Fan intensity scores high on legacy but is held back by a 31-51 rebuild and ownership fatigue. Near-term upside is in civic and outerwear product, mostly in the 2027-28 cycle, more than in current-player demand.

music.headline: Chicago music runs on inventions, and the Bulls still walk out in the dark.
music.summary: Chicago invented electric blues, gospel, house and footwork, then added drill and a slam-poetry rap line that runs from Common to Chance the Rapper, Noname and Saba. House is the best story for product, because no other city can claim it. Make that Black-built sound with the DJs, poets and dancers who own it. Drill is tied to real violence and an active federal case, and R. Kelly and Kanye West are off-limits.

insights.title: House was born under two miles from the United Center
insights.detail: House got its name at The Warehouse, 206 S. Jefferson St., where Frankie Knuckles played from 1977. Ron Hardy took it rawer at the Music Box. WBMX's Hot Mix 5 radio mixes carried it into every South and West Side home. The block is now signed Frankie Knuckles Way, and the city marks Aug 25 as Frankie Knuckles Day.
insights.implication: House is the Bulls' most swap-proof cultural export, and it comes from the team's own side of town. Anchor a city collection on it, co-made with house institutions like the Chosen Few DJs. Don't borrow it as a party aesthetic.

insights.title: The Bulls' anthem is a lights-out ritual
insights.detail: Since the mid-1980s, the Bulls have introduced their starters in a darkened arena with roving spotlights. The soundtrack is the Alan Parsons Project's 1982 instrumental 'Sirius.' Ray Clay's 1990s calls made it one of the most imitated intros in sports. It ties Jordan's Chicago Stadium, 'the Madhouse on Madison,' to the current rebuild.
insights.implication: The darkness, the spotlight beams and the red glow belong to the Bulls and need no music license. They make strong cues for reflective or glow-in-the-dark pregame and warmup product. Don't name or use the song without clearance.

insights.title: Slam poetry shaped Chicago rap as much as drill did
insights.detail: Slam poetry was invented at Uptown's Green Mill in 1986. In the early 2010s, YOUmedia, the teen studio at Harold Washington Library, and Young Chicago Authors' Louder Than a Bomb slam were the pipeline. Out of it came Chance the Rapper, Noname, Saba, Mick Jenkins and Jamila Woods. Common, son of ABA player Lonnie Lynn, set the conscious-rap template in the 1990s.
insights.implication: Wordplay is the scene's real craft. Give Bulls product type-led graphics and copy written by paid local poet-rappers. Sponsor the youth creative pipeline instead of mining street mythology.

insights.title: The South and West Sides built dances that are sneaker culture
insights.detail: Footwork is the 160-BPM dance and music that grew out of ghetto house and juke battles. RP Boo and DJ Rashad and DJ Spinn's Teklife crew pushed it worldwide. Chicago stepping is the smooth partner dance of Black Chicago's adult lounges and steppers' sets. Both live or die on footwear.
insights.implication: Footwork dancers are natural wear-testers and content creators for a Bulls-colored low-top court shoe. Turn the dance's foot-placement patterns into graphics. Partner with the crews and pay them. Don't just cast them.

insights.title: Drill made Chicago famous and is the riskiest sound to touch
insights.detail: Chief Keef's 2012 'I Don't Like' and 'Love Sosa,' recorded around Parkway Gardens ('O-Block') in Woodlawn, turned Chicago drill into a global style. The genre is tied to real killings, such as King Von's in 2020. Lil Durk was arrested on federal murder-for-hire charges in 2024.
insights.implication: Drill shapes how young Chicago dresses, but stay out of its imagery, slang and artists. Reach the same audience through DJs, producers, dancers and sneaker culture.

insights.title: Blues and gospel give the market a heritage palette
insights.detail: Muddy Waters, Howlin' Wolf and Willie Dixon electrified Delta blues at Chess Records, 2120 S. Michigan Ave., now Willie Dixon's Blues Heaven Foundation. Thomas A. Dorsey created gospel music at Pilgrim Baptist in Bronzeville. Buddy Guy, who turned 90 in July 2026, still anchors the South Loop at Legends.
insights.implication: Build a vintage capsule on club neon and record-label type. Release it around the free Chicago Blues Festival in June, and share proceeds with Blues Heaven. Don't lift Chess marks.

insights.title: A new roster with no music face yet
insights.detail: We know of no public Chicago music ties for anyone in the new core of Giddey, No. 4 pick Caleb Wilson, Norman Powell and Nic Claxton. Chicago-born Matas Buzelis is the one hometown thread. The team's last big music moment was the 2020 All-Star Game at the United Center. Chance played the halftime show, Common spoke the intros and Chaka Khan sang the anthem.
insights.implication: Build the team's tie to the scene from scratch. Pair Buzelis and Wilson with local artists for content and launches. Treat the 2020 all-local lineup, a Chicago-only bill that carried the night, as the template for a home-opener music moment.

places.name: Willie Dixon's Blues Heaven Foundation (former Chess Records)
places.neighborhood: Near South Side (Record Row, 2120 S. Michigan Ave.)
places.why: Where Chicago electric blues and early rock 'n' roll were recorded. Dixon's foundation now runs it, which makes it the city's most credible heritage partner.

places.name: Frankie Knuckles Way (site of The Warehouse, 206 S. Jefferson St.)
places.why: The club where house was born and named, less than two miles east of the United Center on the same side of town.

places.name: Smart Bar
places.why: A house and techno basement club since 1982, where Chicago's DJ lineage still plays every week. The right room for an after-hours launch.

places.name: Gramaphone Records
places.why: The dance-music shop where Chicago house DJs have dug for 12-inch records for decades.

places.name: Dusty Groove
places.neighborhood: Ukrainian Village / Wicker Park (N. Ashland Ave.)
places.why: A soul, jazz and funk crate-digger institution. Its sleeve-art archive is a visual reference library for Chicago soul.

places.name: Green Mill Cocktail Lounge
places.why: A 1907 jazz room with a famous green neon sign. Its Sunday-night Uptown Poetry Slam, started in 1986, invented slam poetry.

places.name: Buddy Guy's Legends
places.why: Buddy Guy's own club, still the city's flagship blues room. He plays an annual January residency here.

places.name: Harold Washington Library Center (YOUmedia)
places.why: The teen studio and open mic where Chance, Noname and Saba came up, and the origin point of Chicago's 2010s rap renaissance.

places.name: WHPK 88.5 FM
places.why: A long-running University of Chicago community station. Its hip-hop, house and juke shows give South Side DJs a regular platform.

people.name: Chosen Few DJs
people.role: House DJ collective founded by Wayne Williams
people.why: Its Jackson Park picnic, often called the 'Woodstock of house,' is Black Chicago's house family reunion. Any house capsule needs the collective as co-creator.

people.name: Chance the Rapper
people.role: Rapper from West Chatham and founder of SocialWorks
people.why: A YOUmedia alumnus and lifelong Chicago booster who headlined the 2020 All-Star halftime show at the United Center. He is the most recognizable bridge between the scene and the arena.

people.name: Common
people.role: South Side rapper and actor; Grammy and Oscar winner
people.why: The son of an ABA player, he gave the spoken-word player intros at the 2020 All-Star Game. He is the elder statesman of Chicago's conscious, wordplay-first lineage.

people.name: Saba (Pivot Gang)
people.role: Rapper and producer from Austin on the West Side
people.why: He comes from the United Center's side of town. 'Care for Me' and his recent work with producer No I.D. make him the respected local voice of the current era.

people.name: Ravyn Lenae
people.role: South Side R&B singer and Chicago High School for the Arts alumna
people.why: 'Love Me Not' made her one of the city's biggest breakout stars of 2025: a rising, non-drill face who reaches young fans.

people.name: Teklife
people.role: Footwork crew and label founded by DJ Rashad and DJ Spinn
people.why: Teklife has kept footwork going since Rashad's death in 2014, which makes it the right partner for dance-led sneaker content.

people.name: Honey Dijon
people.role: Chicago-raised (born in Newark) house DJ, producer and fashion designer
people.why: She won a Grammy as a producer on Beyoncé's 'Renaissance' and has collaborated with Comme des Garçons. She is the scene's proven bridge from house to fashion.

people.name: Brandon Breaux
people.why: He made the artwork for Chance's 'Acid Rap,' the defining album art of Chicago's 2010s rap wave. He would be a natural illustrator for a Bulls city collection.

moments.name: Lights-out starting-lineup intro ('Sirius')
moments.why: The Bulls' signature sonic ritual since the Jordan era, and the moment to light up pregame product.

moments.name: Buddy Guy's January residency at Legends
moments.why: A month-long pilgrimage to the living link to Chess-era blues, right in the heart of the Bulls' home schedule.

moments.name: Sueños Music Festival
moments.why: Chicago's big reggaeton and Latin festival, and the best way to reach the city's large Mexican and Puerto Rican fan base.

moments.name: Chicago Blues Festival
moments.why: A free festival since 1984, and the natural release window for a Record Row heritage capsule.

moments.name: Chosen Few DJs Picnic & Festival
moments.why: Tens of thousands of house heads in a family-reunion setting, where Chicago-flag house tees are the unofficial uniform.

moments.name: Bud Billiken Parade
moments.timing: Second Saturday of August, King Drive to Washington Park
moments.why: One of the country's oldest and largest Black parades, running since 1929, powered by South Side drumlines, marching bands and dance troupes.

moments.name: Frankie Knuckles Day
moments.why: The city's official day for the Godfather of House, and a credible restock date for a house capsule.

moments.name: ARC Music Festival
moments.why: A house and techno festival a short drive from the United Center, a few weeks before Bulls preseason.

vocabulary.meaning: The dance music named for The Warehouse. A 'house head' is a lifelong devotee, often of the picnic-going generation.
The original house dance and its verb: a full-body pulse to the beat, as in Steve 'Silk' Hurley's 'Jack Your Body.'
The fast South and West Side dance-battle style and its 160-BPM music. 'Juke' is the earlier party sound it grew out of.
Chicago-style stepping: a smooth partner dance done at steppers' sets in Black adult lounges, to classic R&B.
WBMX's Hot Mix 5 radio mixes of the 1980s, taped off the air onto cassettes and passed around. Shorthand for old-school Chicago mixing.
The stretch of South Michigan Avenue where Chess, Vee-Jay and other labels pressed Chicago blues, soul and doo-wop in the 1950s and '60s.
Chicago Stadium, the Bulls' Jordan-era home across Madison Street from the United Center. It was famous for crowd noise and its thundering Barton pipe organ.
The Chicago-born street-rap style. Learn its slang and set references so you can keep them off product.

designCues.cue: Spotlight red on blackout: Bulls red in a single roving beam against a darkened arena, straight from the lights-out intro
designCues.source: The Bulls' 'Sirius' starting-lineup intro, from Chicago Stadium to the United Center
designCues.use: Print reflective or glow-in-the-dark spotlight beams in Bulls red on near-black (#0B0B0B) warm-ups, so they flare under the intro lights. No song name or lyric needed.

designCues.cue: House-flag light blue: the Chicago flag's sky blue, as reworked on house-music picnic tees
designCues.source: Chicago-flag 'House Music' tees worn at the Chosen Few Picnic and around the house scene
designCues.use: Use it as the base for a house capsule, with red six-point stars (#FF0000) reworked as record centers. Co-design with house DJs. Don't copy fan bootlegs.

designCues.cue: Uptown neon green: the glowing tube script of the city's old music-room signs
designCues.source: The Green Mill's neon sign and the neon signage of South and North Side blues clubs
designCues.use: Use a small accent of neon-tube embroidered script on a heritage blues and jazz capsule. Spell out original words only, and never copy club marks without permission.

designCues.cue: 1980s house-party flyer typography: heavy condensed sans, hand-ruled boxes, stacked date and time lines ending in 'til ?', with toner bleed
designCues.source: Photocopied flyers for The Warehouse, the Music Box and Hot Mix 5 parties
designCues.use: Set pregame-tee graphics in this style for Bulls home dates. Have Chicago designers direct the art, and credit the flyer archivists the team draws from.

designCues.cue: Roster as mixtape: a cassette J-card layout listing the 2026-27 core as a tracklist
designCues.source: Hot Mix cassette culture and the city's 2010s free-mixtape era (Acid Rap, Coloring Book)
designCues.use: Use it on a rebuild-era tee or hangtag, paired with a real mix by a local DJ released as launch content.

designCues.cue: Footwork foot-placement diagram on a 160-BPM rhythm grid
designCues.source: Footwork battle circles on the South and West Sides
designCues.use: Print it on insoles, socks and shorts for a footwork-tested low-top, built with paid input from Teklife and other footwork crews.

designCues.cue: Record Row to Madison Street: a route map linking Chess on South Michigan, The Warehouse on Jefferson, and the Stadium and United Center on Madison
designCues.source: The geography of Chicago's music inventions alongside the Bulls' homes
designCues.use: Print it as an inside-collar or hangtag story that puts the Bulls inside the city's music history.

productHooks: 'Born in Chicago' house capsule: a Bulls pregame shooting shirt and tee in house-flag blue with Warehouse-flyer type. Co-design it with the Chosen Few DJs and pay them. Release it at the July picnic and restock on Frankie Knuckles Day (Aug 25).
Lights-out 'Spotlight' warmup: a near-black jacket with reflective Bulls-red beam graphics that flare during the United Center intro. Launch it at the 2026-27 home opener.
Footwork-tested low-top: a Nike Basketball low in Bulls colors with a rhythm-grid insole. Teklife and other footwork crews wear-test it and launch it at a South or West Side battle.
'Rebuild Mixtape' tee: Giddey, Buzelis, Wilson, Powell and Claxton as a cassette tracklist, sold with a mix by a Chicago DJ and a halftime set at the United Center.

Record Row heritage capsule for the June Blues Fest: a vintage-wash tee and coaches jacket with original label-style graphics and neon-script accents. Share proceeds with Willie Dixon's Blues Heaven Foundation.
City-pack copy and art from the open-mic pipeline: commission Young Chicago Authors and YOUmedia poets to write the copy and Brandon Breaux to illustrate it, with a spoken-word halftime moment.
watchouts: Drill is tied to real killings and active feuds. Lil Durk was federally charged with murder-for-hire in 2024 (case status unverified). Keep drill slang, set and block references (O-Block, 'on foenem,' 'Chiraq') and its artists off product and out of content.

R. Kelly, who is convicted and wrote 'I Believe I Can Fly' for Space Jam, and Kanye West, after his antisemitic statements and the adidas split, are off-limits. That includes Jordan-era nostalgia, playlists and archival footage.

'Sirius' is Alan Parsons Project IP, and also a SiriusXM mark. Chess, Trax and Dance Mania label art, the band Chicago's logo, Lyrical Lemonade branding and Frankie Knuckles' name and likeness all need clearance. Design originals or license.

Black and Latino queer DJs and dancers built house at The Warehouse. Telling it as a generic 'Chicago party' erases them. Credit and pay Black and queer DJs, consult the Knuckles estate and the Chosen Few, and don't limit it to Pride-month timing.
Check rival-brand deals before any partnership. Derrick Rose, Englewood's hometown hero, is a longtime adidas athlete, and artist footwear and apparel deals change fast.

art.headline: Chicago dresses in civic graphics and painted the country's first community mural.
art.summary: Chicago's look is civic and systematic: flag stars, grid-numbered street signs, L lines by color. Its walls carry the country's deepest community-mural lineage, from the 1967 Wall of Respect to Pilsen and Paseo Boricua. With a new regime building around Giddey, Buzelis and Wilson, keep the unchanged 1966 bull and let living Chicago artists draw the new era.

insights.title: Chicago invented the community mural
insights.detail: In 1967, visual artists of the Organization of Black American Culture (OBAC) painted the Wall of Respect at 43rd and Langley in Bronzeville. It was a 'heroes' wall, with a sports panel beside its jazz, literature and statesmen sections. It started the community-mural movement, which led to William Walker and John Pitman Weber's Chicago Mural Group (later Chicago Public Art Group) in 1971.
insights.implication: In Chicago a mural is a neighborhood-owned civic statement, not an ad wall. Commission any Bulls or Nike mural from South and West Side muralists and credit them by name. It can openly cite the Wall of Respect lineage.

insights.title: AfriCOBRA made Chicago art wearable
insights.detail: AfriCOBRA was founded on the South Side in 1968 by Jeff Donaldson, Wadsworth Jarrell, Jae Jarrell, Barbara Jones-Hogu and Gerald Williams. It wrote a visual code: 'Kool-Aid colors', shine, free symmetry, and lettering woven into the figures. Jae Jarrell's 'Revolutionary Suit' made it literal clothing.
insights.implication: No other NBA city has an art movement this native to apparel. Build Black History Month product on AfriCOBRA principles, through licensed work with surviving members and estates. Skip generic Pan-African graphics.

insights.title: The city's civic graphics already work as fan gear
insights.detail: The flag's four six-pointed stars are probably the city's most common tattoo, and its three white bands stand for the North, West and South Sides. Street signs carry the grid number (Halsted 800 W, Ashland 1600 W, Damen 2000 W), and honorary street signs are brown. Even the city vehicle sticker has been designed by high-school students, through the City Clerk's contest.
insights.implication: Fans already treat municipal design as identity, but flag tees are everywhere. The less-used codes are open territory for City Edition and capsule work: grid numbers, brown honorary signs, the L palette and Sullivan ornament.

insights.title: Pilsen and Humboldt Park paint in their own idiom
insights.detail: Pilsen's walls carry Mexican muralism, from the 16th Street rail embankment to Hector Duarte's studio mural. The National Museum of Mexican Art's Día de Muertos exhibition anchors it. On Division Street, two 1995 steel Puerto Rican flags mark Paseo Boricua. Pilsen also remembers fights over protecting older murals, such as Casa Aztlán's.
insights.implication: Latino fan product must be authored by these communities: commissioned, paid, credited and launched in the neighborhood. Avoid gentrification optics. A brand mural that overwrites local work would be a crisis.

insights.title: Chicago's streetwear bench is split between Nike and its competitors
insights.detail: Don C and Virgil Abloh opened RSVP Gallery in Wicker Park in 2009. Don C went on to Jordan Brand collaborations (the Air Jordan 2 'Just Don', the Legacy 312). The MCA debuted Abloh's 'Figures of Speech' in 2019. Joe Freshgoods, the city's most-followed current streetwear voice, makes his Chicago-story releases with New Balance.
insights.implication: Nike's Chicago credibility runs through Jordan Brand, but the next bench is open. Scout SAIC fashion students and the Columbia College and Wabash Arts Corridor scene. Don't chase a competitor's partner.

insights.title: Chicago has its own pop art: the Imagists
insights.detail: The Hairy Who (Jim Nutt, Gladys Nilsson, Karl Wirsum, Suellen Rocca, Art Green, James Falconer) showed at the Hyde Park Art Center from 1966 to 1969. Their crude comic-book line and carnival color, along with Ed Paschke's neon-drenched portraits, are the city's homegrown visual dialect.
insights.implication: Imagism is a Chicago-only alternative to generic graffiti graphics, and it suits a young, gangly, physical 'SLAP' roster. License estates or brief living artists in the idiom, ideally through the Hyde Park Art Center.

insights.title: A logo that never changed and a statue that never left
insights.detail: Chicago commercial artist Dean Wessel is credited with the charging-bull mark in 1966, and it has never been redesigned. 'The Spirit', the 1994 Jordan statue by Omri Amrany and Julie Rotblatt-Amrany from their Highland Park studio, still anchors the United Center.
insights.implication: Keep the bull as the fixed point. Let new Chicago art carry the new era of coach Tiago Splitter, EVP Bryson Graham and a core of Josh Giddey, Matas Buzelis and Caleb Wilson. In a rebuild year, fans will read another '90s throwback cycle as filler.

places.name: Pilsen murals (16th Street rail embankment and 18th Street)
places.why: The city's densest run of murals, where Mexican muralism meets graffiti writers along a long stretch of embankment wall.

places.name: National Museum of Mexican Art
places.why: Carlos Tortolero's free museum runs one of the country's largest Día de Muertos exhibitions. It is the institutional partner for Mexican-Chicago artists.

places.name: Paseo Boricua steel flags
places.neighborhood: Humboldt Park (Division St between Western and California)
places.why: Two 1995 steel Puerto Rican flags arch over Division Street: the city's boldest piece of community-made graphic architecture.

places.name: Wabash Arts Corridor
places.why: Columbia College Chicago's mural program, running since 2013, turns Wabash Avenue under the L into a commissioned big-wall gallery. It is a working route for a sanctioned Bulls wall.

places.name: South Side Community Art Center
places.why: A WPA-era center dedicated by Eleanor Roosevelt in 1941, linked to Margaret Burroughs, Charles White and Gordon Parks. It is often called the oldest Black art center in the US.

places.name: Stony Island Arts Bank
places.why: Theaster Gates's restored bank holds the Johnson Publishing (Ebony/Jet) library and Frankie Knuckles' records. It is a Black Chicago visual archive that a design team should visit.

places.name: Hyde Park Art Center
places.why: Founded in 1939, it launched the Hairy Who and still runs classes and residencies. A credible partner for Imagist-inflected work.

places.name: RSVP Gallery
places.why: The original 2009 Don C and Virgil Abloh shop, which shaped Chicago's art-meets-sneaker culture. A live search suggests RSVP now operates in the West Loop (Sangamon St), so confirm the address.

places.name: Sullivan Center (former Carson Pirie Scott)
places.why: Louis Sullivan's cast-iron ornament wraps the corner where the city's address grid begins. Chicago's signature pattern sits on its zero point.

places.name: United Center atrium ('The Spirit')
places.neighborhood: Near West Side (1901 W Madison St)
places.why: Home of the 1994 Jordan statue and the obvious stage for unveiling commissioned art.

people.name: Don C (Just Don)
people.role: Chicago designer; co-founder of RSVP Gallery
people.why: His Jordan Brand work (the AJ2 'Just Don', the Legacy 312) shows that Chicago luxury-streetwear credibility can come from inside the Nike family.

people.name: Joe Freshgoods
people.why: The loudest current voice turning Chicago stories into product, through New Balance. Treat him as a benchmark and a conflict check, not a likely partner.

people.name: Hebru Brantley
people.why: His goggled 'Flyboy' character, a nod to the Tuskegee Airmen, is a recognizable South Side-rooted pop icon with a record of brand collaborations.

people.name: Nick Cave
people.why: His Soundsuits are wearable sculpture, and the MCA mounted his 2022 retrospective 'Forothermore'. He would be a high-art partner for an arena installation or elevated capsule.

people.name: Theaster Gates (Rebuild Foundation)
people.role: Artist and South Side cultural developer
people.why: He runs the Stony Island Arts Bank and its Black Chicago archives. Working with him signals real investment on the South Side, not a borrowed aesthetic.

people.name: AfriCOBRA
people.why: Its 'Kool-Aid colors' and lettering principles are the most apparel-ready art code of any NBA city. License through surviving members and estates.

people.name: Omri Amrany and Julie Rotblatt-Amrany
people.why: They made 'The Spirit' and many NBA statues since: the local makers behind the Bulls' most photographed monument.

people.name: Hector Duarte
people.why: A long-working Pilsen muralist and printmaker with murals across the neighborhood. A credible lead for a Noche Latina commission (confirm availability).

moments.name: Open House Chicago
moments.timing: A mid-October weekend, the week of tipoff
moments.why: The Chicago Architecture Center's free tour of more than 100 buildings puts the city's design vernacular in the spotlight just as the season starts.

moments.name: Día de Muertos at the National Museum of Mexican Art
moments.timing: Exhibition from early fall to early December; holiday Nov 1-2
moments.why: The anchor date for Mexican-Chicago fan product and Noche Latina work, launched in Pilsen with Pilsen artists.

moments.name: Black History Month
moments.why: The moment to bring the Wall of Respect and AfriCOBRA lineage to court, with the South Side Community Art Center, DuSable Black History Museum and Stony Island Arts Bank.

moments.name: Chicago River dyeing
moments.why: Since 1962, Plumbers Local 130 has turned the river an unreal emerald. It is Chicago's most-photographed color moment and a natural cue for a limited 'River Green' drop.

moments.name: EXPO CHICAGO
moments.why: The city's international art fair, now under Frieze, lands as the regular season ends. Announce an artist series here.

moments.name: Chicago Arts District 2nd Fridays
moments.timing: Second Friday evening of each month
moments.why: Pilsen's open-studio night around Halsted and 18th, a standing way to scout and meet working artists.

vocabulary.meaning: The CTA's elevated and subway rail. The Loop is named for the ring of track around downtown. Lines go by color: Red, Blue, Brown, Green, Orange, Pink, Purple, Yellow.

vocabulary.term: The four stars / the fifth star
vocabulary.meaning: The flag's stars mark Fort Dearborn, the 1871 Fire, the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition and the 1933 Century of Progress. Chicagoans periodically campaign for a fifth.
The zero point of the address grid. Every address counts out from here at about 800 numbers per mile, so locals give directions by number ('it's at 2400 West').
Area-code shorthand: 312 is downtown, 773 is the neighborhoods. Both are worn as identity, as in Jordan Brand's Legacy 312.
The city's signature housing: brick two-unit buildings and limestone-faced greystones lining neighborhood blocks.
The winter custom of saving a shoveled parking spot with a lawn chair, cone or laundry basket. Beloved and argued over, it runs through basketball season.
AfriCOBRA's name for its saturated, luminous palette, one of the movement's founding principles.
Chicago's 1960s-70s homegrown pop: comic-strip line, grotesque humor and loud color, as distinct from New York Pop Art.

designCues.cue: Flag Blue: the pale lake-and-river blue of the 1917 Chicago flag, set against Bulls red #CE1141 and black.
designCues.source: Wallace Rice's municipal flag. The two blue stripes are Lake Michigan and the North Branch, and the South Branch and canal. The three white bands are the North, West and South Sides.
designCues.use: Use it in the flag's proportions, as twin pinstripes on side panels, waistbands or collar tape. Skip full-flag prints, which every bootleg tee already uses.

designCues.cue: The Chicago star: a six-pointed red star with long, narrow points, used singly or as a row of four.
designCues.source: The flag's stars, each marking a civic milestone. Fans already connect six points with six championships.
designCues.use: Put one star on a jock tag or waistband medallion that carries a 'six points' championship story. Keep the flag's exact star geometry. Never add a fifth star for a rebuilding team.

designCues.cue: The L palette: Red #C60C30, Blue #00A1DE, Brown #62361B, Green #009B3A, Orange #F9461C, Pink #E27EA6, Purple #522398, Yellow #F9E300.
designCues.source: CTA rail line colors, which riders read as neighborhood identity. The Red Line runs from Howard on the North Side to 95th on the South Side.
designCues.use: Use the colors as a stripe system or a line-per-colorway series, with terminal-stop names as the type. CTA signage and marks need a license.

designCues.cue: Street-sign typography: white condensed sans on green with the hundred-block grid number in the corner, plus the brown signs used for honorary streets.
designCues.source: Chicago street-name signs, which carry grid coordinates (Madison 0 N/S, Damen 2000 W) and set the city's everyday lettering.
designCues.use: Build a number and wordmark lockup around '1901 W Madison', the United Center's address. Use brown 'honorary' signs to salute legends on tees and neck tape.

designCues.cue: Sullivan ornament: interlaced foliage and geometric cast-iron scrollwork.
designCues.source: Louis Sullivan's corner rotunda at the Sullivan Center (State and Madison) and the Auditorium Building. Chicago School architecture is the city's design signature.
designCues.use: Use it as a tonal jacquard, debossed trim or knit pattern in black-on-black or red-on-red. The buildings are public, but redraw the pattern instead of scanning photographs.

designCues.cue: AfriCOBRA code: saturated 'Kool-Aid' color, light-catching shine, and words built into the figures.
designCues.source: The South Side collective founded in 1968, extending the Wall of Respect's heroes tradition.
designCues.use: Use it for Black History Month graphics, with lettering built into player and fan imagery. Commission or license through AfriCOBRA members and estates, with credit and pay.

designCues.cue: Marquee and neon lettering: stacked vertical letters with bulb-dot and neon-tube outlines.
designCues.source: The Chicago Theatre's vertical 'CHICAGO' sign on State Street, the Green Mill's neon in Uptown and Superdawg's rooftop figures in Norwood Park.
designCues.use: Run a vertical 'CHICAGO' stack down a sleeve or side panel with a bulb-dot texture. Draw original letterforms and don't copy the theatre's trademarked sign.

designCues.cue: L steel and common brick: riveted girder grids and the irregular salmon-to-buff Chicago common brick of two-flats.
designCues.source: The Loop's 1890s elevated structure and the bungalow-belt and two-flat blocks.
designCues.use: Use a rivet-grid emboss on taping and outerwear yokes and a tonal brick-bond jacquard on fleece, for winter product that feels like a Chicago block.

productHooks: '1901 W' grid pack: shooting shirt, hoodie and cap in Chicago street-sign type (white on green), with Flag Blue pinstripes and each player's number shown as a grid coordinate. Commission the lettering from a Chicago type designer.

Wall of Respect / AfriCOBRA Black History Month capsule in 'Kool-Aid' color with integrated lettering, licensed from members and estates. Launch it at the South Side Community Art Center and share proceeds with it.

'Ride the L' series: eight colorways of tees and crew socks under a CTA license, one per line, with terminal stops as typography. Lead with the Red Line (Howard to 95th) as the North-to-South Bulls unifier.

Noche Latina drop around Día de Muertos: commission a Pilsen muralist such as Hector Duarte, work with the National Museum of Mexican Art and release it in Pilsen. Use original artwork, not stock calaveras.
New-era wall: an artist-led mural of Giddey, Buzelis and Caleb Wilson on the Wabash Arts Corridor, unveiled on Open House Chicago weekend. Add a limited print-and-tee run credited to the muralist.
watchouts: Brand conflicts: Joe Freshgoods works with New Balance, and Virgil Abloh's legacy is managed by his estate and the brands he led. Check exclusivity before approaching any Chicago designer, and avoid 'poaching' optics.

Third-party IP needs a license or a full redraw. That covers CTA marks and signage, the Chicago Theatre sign, Morton Salt's umbrella girl, Vienna Beef and the Wrigley Field marquee (a Cubs asset). 'The Spirit' carries the sculptors' copyright plus Jordan's likeness.

Community authorship: Pilsen's murals, Día de Muertos ofrendas and calaveras, Mexica and Indigenous imagery, and the Puerto Rican flag are not decoration. Commission, credit and pay artists from those communities. Never paint over or crowd out existing murals. Casa Aztlán is still remembered.
Don't use 'Chiraq', drill-scene shorthand or violence tropes, and don't show the South and West Sides only through hardship. Use their artists, institutions and joy.
The flag and four stars are saturated in bootleg merch and carry specific civic meanings. Execute them precisely. Never invent a fifth star to manufacture hype for a rebuilding team.

verify: Check which civic motifs (flag stars, Flag Blue, CTA colors, grid numbers, marquee lettering) the 2025-26 and 2026-27 Bulls City Edition designs already use, so new concepts don't repeat them.
Confirm Joe Freshgoods' current brand partnership (New Balance) and Don C's current Jordan Brand relationship as of 2026.
Confirm 'The Spirit' is still displayed in the United Center atrium, and how image rights work with the Rotblatt-Amrany studio and Jordan.
Confirm Open House Chicago 2026 dates (expected mid-October) and building list.
Confirm the National Museum of Mexican Art's 2026 Día de Muertos exhibition dates.
Confirm RSVP Gallery is still operating in Wicker Park.
Check Stony Island Arts Bank and South Side Community Art Center 2026-27 public hours and partnership contacts.
Confirm EXPO CHICAGO 2027 dates, venue (Navy Pier in recent editions) and ownership.
Confirm Chicago Arts District 2nd Fridays is still running in Pilsen.
Check the Wabash Arts Corridor's current commissioning process and available walls.
Confirm the City Clerk's student vehicle-sticker design contest is still running.
Check CTA licensing terms for using line colors and station signage on apparel.

food.headline: Chicago eats standing up, and nobody puts ketchup on the dog.
food.summary: Chicago food is working-class, neighborhood-owned and eaten fast. Italian beef, Chicago dogs and tavern-cut pizza share the city with a Black-owned South Side canon and immigrant corridors that give each side of town its own menu. Game day is a pre-game dinner, not a tailgate. In a rebuild year, food is a low-risk way for Nike to show neighborhood pride, as long as the stands are paid, credited and licensed.

insights.title: The Chicago dog already wears Bulls colors
insights.detail: A Chicago dog is an all-beef frank on a poppy-seed bun with yellow mustard, neon-green relish, onion, tomato wedges, a pickle spear, sport peppers and celery salt. That's 'dragged through the garden,' and asking for ketchup gets you mocked. Locals defend Superdawg (Norwood Park, 1948) and Gene & Jude's in River Grove, which piles fries on top and has no seats.
insights.implication: Tomato red and poppy-seed black are Bulls red and black. A hot-dog accent pack (neon relish, mustard, seed speckle) reads as Chicago without a literal food graphic. 'No ketchup' is the insider joke a hangtag or insole can carry.

insights.title: Italian beef is ordered in code
insights.detail: At Al's #1 on Taylor Street (since 1938), Johnnie's in Elmwood Park and Mr. Beef on Orleans, you order 'sweet or hot,' meaning roasted peppers or giardiniera. You also pick 'dry, juicy or dipped,' and 'combo,' which is beef plus sausage. You eat in 'the Italian stance,' leaning over the counter so the jus misses your shirt. FX's The Bear, modeled on Mr. Beef, took that vocabulary national.
insights.implication: The order code is a ready-made naming and colorway system (Dipped, Hot, Combo) for a fan pack. Beef-stand workwear cues (aprons, deli paper, order stamps) land right now. Draw from the real stands and pay them. The Bear's names and marks are FX/Disney IP.

insights.title: Locals eat tavern-cut, visitors eat deep dish
insights.detail: The everyday Chicago pizza is cracker-thin tavern style, cut into squares (the 'party cut'), from South Side spots like Vito & Nick's in Ashburn. People fight over the crunchy corner pieces. Pequod's caramelized-crust pan pie is the cult exception. Food reporter Steve Dolinsky's book 'Pizza City, USA' argues that tavern style, not deep dish, is the city's real pie.
insights.implication: The square-cut grid is the insider pizza cue. Deep-dish graphics read as airport souvenirs. Chicagoans eat tavern pizza during road games, so it suits a watch-party kit.

insights.title: The South Side canon is Black-owned and number-coded
insights.detail: Harold's Chicken Shack (founded 1950) goes by location number and serves mild sauce over fries and white bread. On 75th Street, Lem's Bar-B-Q smokes rib tips and hot links in a glass-walled 'aquarium' pit. Brown Sugar Bakery down the block sells caramel cake. Erick Williams of Virtue in Hyde Park is the neighborhood's fine-dining voice.
insights.implication: This is the core of a February Black History Month food story. Build it as paid, credited partnerships with these owners. Never borrow their logos or turn chicken and barbecue into a punchline.

insights.title: Immigrant corridors map the city
insights.detail: Pilsen's 18th Street (Carnitas Uruapan, since 1975) and Little Village's 26th Street anchor Mexican Chicago. The jibarito, a steak sandwich with fried plantains for bread, was created in Humboldt Park in 1996 and lives along Paseo Boricua. Patel Brothers opened its first store on Devon Avenue in 1974. Polish bakeries line Milwaukee Avenue.
insights.implication: Co-design neighborhood capsules corridor by corridor, with local businesses and cultural groups. Time them to heritage nights and summer festivals. Skip the one generic 'Chicago food' print.

insights.title: Game day is a pre-game dinner, not a tailgate
insights.detail: The United Center (1901 W. Madison) sits inside a food triangle. Randolph Street and Fulton Market, a mile east, have Au Cheval and Girl & the Goat. Greektown is on Halsted, and Taylor Street is Little Italy. Jim's Original Maxwell Street Polish stand is near UIC. In winter, Bulls fans eat before tip-off instead of tailgating in the lots.
insights.implication: Stage launch nights indoors inside that triangle, such as a Fulton Market pop-up or collab wrappers at Al's on City Edition nights. Design for fans commuting in coats over jerseys on the No. 20 Madison bus or the L plus a long walk.

insights.title: The rebuild has a hometown pantry
insights.detail: Matas Buzelis is a Chicago-area native of Lithuanian heritage, and greater Chicago has one of the largest Lithuanian communities outside Lithuania. Think cepelinai dumplings and spit-baked sakotis 'tree cake.' Coach Tiago Splitter and EVP Graham are starting over around Josh Giddey, Buzelis and Caleb Wilson. Expectations are low, so homegrown stories carry more than win totals.
insights.implication: A Buzelis-fronted community night with Lithuanian-American bakeries and organizations gives local fans a reason to buy in during a rebuild. Confirm his community ties and get their buy-in before concepting.

places.name: Al's #1 Italian Beef
places.why: The 1938 original of the city's signature sandwich, a short ride from the United Center and the natural pre-game beef stop.

places.name: Mr. Beef on Orleans
places.why: The counter that inspired FX's The Bear, now a pilgrimage stop for out-of-town fans.

places.name: Superdawg Drive-In
places.why: A 1948 carhop drive-in with rooftop hot dog figures Maurie and Flaurie, the North Side's best-known stand.

places.name: Gene & Jude's
places.why: No seats, no ketchup, fries piled on the dog: the purist's 'depression dog' since 1946.

places.name: Lem's Bar-B-Q
places.why: Rib tips and hot links from an aquarium smoker, the defining South Side barbecue since the 1950s.

places.name: Vito & Nick's Pizzeria
places.why: A Southwest Side tavern-style institution and the benchmark for thin, square-cut pizza.

places.name: The Original Rainbow Cone
places.why: The pink 1926 shop at 92nd and Western, whose five-flavor cone is a South Side summer ritual.

places.name: Carnitas Uruapan
places.why: Family-run on 18th Street since 1975, it anchors Pilsen's Michoacan-style carnitas tradition.

places.name: Paseo Boricua
places.why: The stretch of Division Street between two steel Puerto Rican flags, home of the jibarito and the center of Puerto Rican Chicago.

places.name: Balzekas Museum of Lithuanian Culture and Lithuanian Plaza
places.why: The institutional home of Lithuanian Chicago, and the community around Matas Buzelis's heritage. Cepelinai and sakotis bakeries cater community nights here. Confirm operating status before building a partnership.

people.name: Harold's Chicken Shack
people.role: Black-owned fried chicken chain founded by Harold Pierce in 1950
people.why: Its numbered locations, mild sauce and hatchet-chef logo are South and West Side shorthand. Any use is a licensing conversation.

people.name: Erick Williams
people.role: Chef-owner of Virtue in Hyde Park
people.why: A James Beard Best Chef: Great Lakes winner and the South Side's most credible chef voice for Black History Month.

people.name: Stephanie Izard
people.role: Chef behind Girl & the Goat; first woman to win Top Chef
people.why: The best-known chef on Randolph Street's pre-game row, with national TV reach.

people.name: Kasama (Tim Flores and Genie Kwon)
people.why: The first Filipino restaurant to earn a Michelin star. Its morning pastry lines make it a cult spot for younger fans.

people.name: Diana Davila
people.role: Chef of Mi Tocaya Antojeria in Logan Square
people.why: A Chicago-raised Mexican-American chef whose regional Mexican cooking speaks for the city's Latino food scene from inside it.

people.name: Steve Dolinsky
people.role: Food reporter ('The Hungry Hound') and author of 'Pizza City, USA'
people.why: The loudest advocate for tavern style as Chicago's real pizza, and a credible guide for a pizza-themed drop.

people.name: Dark Matter Coffee
people.why: Its art-forward bags and artist-collab merch are worn around town. A model for a credited co-branded drop.

people.name: Vienna Beef
people.role: Chicago hot dog maker since the 1893 World's Fair
people.why: Its sign hangs over most of the city's hot dog stands, so its marks define the stand look and require licensing.

moments.name: Pre-game beef or dog run
moments.why: Fans eat on Taylor Street, in Greektown or on Randolph Street before heading to the United Center.

moments.name: Chicago Restaurant Week
moments.why: A citywide prix-fixe run by Choose Chicago, mid-season and leading into Black History Month. It frames a Bulls x chef series.

moments.name: Paczki Day
moments.why: Lines form at Polish bakeries along Milwaukee Avenue and in the suburbs, two days before the trade deadline.

moments.name: Puerto Rican Fest and People's Parade
moments.why: Humboldt Park's biggest weekend, with jibaritos and lechon along Paseo Boricua.

moments.name: Fiesta del Sol
moments.why: Pilsen's long-running Mexican street festival, which overlaps Summer League.

moments.name: Bud Billiken Parade and Picnic
moments.why: A back-to-school South Side parade that ends in Washington Park cookouts, and the biggest Black Chicago gathering of the summer.

moments.name: Taste of Chicago
moments.why: The city's signature food festival now lands just before preseason, a launch window for tip-off product.

moments.name: Chicago Gourmet
moments.why: The chef festival in Millennium Park, where the city's restaurant names gather before the season.

vocabulary.meaning: A Chicago dog with all seven toppings and celery salt, never ketchup.
Italian beef order: the whole sandwich dunked in jus, topped with hot giardiniera. 'Juicy' is a lighter dunk. 'Sweet' means roasted green peppers.
Italian beef plus a char-grilled Italian sausage in the same roll.
Leaning over the counter, elbows out, so a dripping beef misses your clothes.
Oil-packed hot giardiniera, the city's all-purpose condiment on beef, pizza and eggs.
Thin-crust pizza cut into squares instead of wedges. The corner pieces are prized.
The sweet, tangy red sauce poured over wings and fries at South and West Side chicken shacks.
A Puerto Rican sandwich that uses flattened fried plantains as the bread. Born in Humboldt Park.

designCues.cue: Neon Relish: the electric green of Chicago dog relish as a small, loud accent against Bulls red #CE1141 and black.
designCues.source: The dyed sweet relish on every Chicago-style hot dog.
designCues.use: Use on pull tabs, aglets, lining and insoles only, so it reads as an insider wink, not a costume.

designCues.cue: Stand Mustard: the bright yellow of the mustard line, paired with Neon Relish for a full hot-dog accent pack.
designCues.source: Yellow mustard squeezed down the dog at stands from Superdawg to Gene & Jude's.
designCues.use: Use for a single piping line or 'mustard stripe' on shorts and warm-ups. Keep stand logos off unless licensed.

designCues.cue: Poppy-seed speckle: tiny black flecks scattered on a toasted-bun cream base (#EBCF9C).
designCues.source: The poppy-seed bun that makes a Chicago dog recognizable.
designCues.use: Use as a speckled midsole, fleece heather or tee print. It doubles as Bulls black on cream.

designCues.cue: Dipped: a deep jus brown with small confetti flecks of giardiniera orange, green and white.
designCues.source: Italian beef soaked in gravy and topped with hot giardiniera.
designCues.use: Use as the base for a 'Dipped / Hot / Combo' hoodie or warm-up pack, with the flecks as a subtle all-over print.

designCues.cue: Tavern-cut grid: an irregular square grid with the crunchy corner piece highlighted, echoing the city's own street grid.
designCues.source: Square-cut thin-crust pizza at South Side taverns like Vito & Nick's.
designCues.use: Use as an all-over print or box-mailer graphic for a watch-party kit, with no restaurant name.

designCues.cue: Rainbow Cone stack: five horizontal bands of chocolate #5B3A29, strawberry #F6A5B8, Palmer House cream #F3E8CF, pistachio #B9D98A and orange sherbet #FF9F45.
designCues.source: The five-flavor cone sold since 1926 at the pink shop on 92nd and Western in Beverly.
designCues.use: Use for a licensed summer, kids' or Summer League capsule, crediting the shop on hangtags.

designCues.cue: Chicago Mix: caramel gold paired with cheddar orange #F28B22 in a half-and-half split.
designCues.source: Caramel-and-cheese popcorn, the city's signature snack.
designCues.use: Use as a split colorway on a sneaker or tee. Avoid any popcorn brand's tins or trade dress, and confirm the name is free to use.

designCues.cue: Aquarium smoker: a glass-walled pit with smoke behind it, rendered as a smoked translucent panel.
designCues.source: The glass-sided smokers at South Side barbecue spots like Lem's on 75th Street.
designCues.use: Use as smoked-tint TPU windows or overlays on a South Side-inspired shoe, built with and credited to the pitmasters.

productHooks: 'Dragged Through the Garden' pack in Bulls red and black, with neon-relish and mustard accents, a poppy-seed speckle and a 'No ketchup' hangtag. Launch it during opening week with a paid, licensed Superdawg or Gene & Jude's pop-up.

'Dipped / Hot / Combo' hoodie and warm-up trio in jus brown with giardiniera flecks. Wrap it in white deli paper with an order-code stamp, and sell it for one night at Al's #1 on Taylor Street on a City Edition home date.

Tavern-cut watch-party kit: a square-grid tee with the corner piece highlighted, plus a pizza-box mailer. Make it with a South Side tavern-style spot for the Bulls' Emirates NBA Cup group games in November.
Black History Month chef series during Chicago Restaurant Week 2027. Erick Williams, Lem's and Brown Sugar Bakery each co-design a menu item and a credited, paid patch or tee for a South Side pop-up.
Rainbow Cone five-stripe summer capsule for kids and Summer League. License it from the Original Rainbow Cone and launch it at the pink shop on 92nd and Western.
Corridor tees co-designed with businesses on Paseo Boricua, 18th Street in Pilsen and Devon Avenue. Sell them through those businesses, with shared revenue, on Bulls heritage nights.
watchouts: Vienna Beef, Superdawg's Maurie and Flaurie, Harold's, Portillo's, Garrett, the Original Rainbow Cone and Mr. Beef all own their logos and trade dress. The Bear belongs to FX/Disney. License and pay, or use generic food cues only.
Keep Malort, Old Style and other alcohol brands off basketball product. It is youth-facing and the NBA restricts alcohol marks, even though 'Malort face' is beloved local humor.

Deep-dish cliches read as tourist merch, and fried-chicken or barbecue jokes read as racist caricature. Black and Latino food cues should come only through paid, credited partnerships with the owners.
The Puerto Rican, Mexican and Lithuanian flags are national symbols, not decoration. Co-design with community organizations and don't mash the flags into Bulls marks.
Neighborhood food spots close or change hands (Hot Doug's shut in 2014). Confirm every partner is open and willing before anything goes on durable product.
